1.explanation: All of these functions form the core of the rendering-tests runner in the rendering folder: webpack.config.js builds the entry list of cases; serve() and main() set up and drive the server+test flow; render() launches Puppeteer; renderEach()/renderPage()/exposeRender() navigate to each test page and capture screenshots; match()/getScreenshotsMismatch() compare actual vs expected images; getOutdated()/getLatest() decide which tests to run. To unify the two approaches, this entire test.js/webpack.config.js machinery must be modified to load and execute both sets of tests in a single runner, so these are the key locations to extend or refactor.
1.bug_scenario: The project currently runs rendering tests in two different ways: one set of tests lives under the rendering directory (using rendering/test.js together with its webpack.config.js and the rendering/cases folder), while another set lives under test/rendering. The images show side-by-side comparisons of “actual.png” vs “expected.png” for each rendering case, with mismatches highlighted. The goal is to unify these two test runners into a single approach.

2.explanation: All of the rendering tests under rendering/ are driven by the functions in rendering/test.js (serve, renderPage, renderEach, render, and main), which set up the test server, run Puppeteer to capture screenshots, compare them, and report results. The webpack.config.js entry generation determines which test cases are built and served. To unify the two testing approaches, these key functions and the entry configuration must be adapted or merged with the existing test/rendering setup so that a single runner and a common set of entries drive every rendering test.
2.bug_scenario: The project currently runs rendering output tests in two separate ways: one is the custom Node‐based test runner under rendering/ (with rendering/test.js and its webpack.config.js), and the other is the suite under test/rendering (not shown here). This split causes duplication, inconsistent behavior, and maintenance overhead. The goal is to unify both test sets into a single, coherent rendering test framework.
